reason: The court merely found the appellants' documents failed to prove their alleged 50-year possession, not that prescription requires possession for more than 50 years.
The burden proposition was applied as part of the decision, but the supplied quote is a quotation from Rasiah v Somapala rather than this court's own supporting language.
The statement reverses the adopted rule, because the court said abandonment of the principal servitude carries the accessory with it, not the other way around.
The privity rule was adopted as necessary to decide the landlord-tenant appeal, but the quote is reproduced Supreme Court authority and SRC029-s58 was not the provision construed.
The court did apply Section 3 of the Prescription Ordinance, but the supplied quote only lists authorities and transitions to the facts rather than stating the rule.
The court stated and applied the Section 3 burden-and-starting-point requirement to reject the defendants' prescriptive claim.
The court formulated this joinder rule for pleaded rights of way and used it to reject the appellant's non-joinder argument.
The decision turned on the judge's Partition Law duties after a doubtful survey return, but the supplied quote is factual and the statement drops the material survey-identity conditions.
The quote supports the factual holding on adverse possession for over ten years, but the statement omits material Section 3 conditions such as undisturbed and uninterrupted possession.
The court construed and applied Civil Procedure Code section 289 to hold that the certificate of sale alone did not pass title without a Fiscal's conveyance.
The court relied on Partition Law section 26(4) and the common-ownership condition when affirming partition of the lands.
The court construed Trusts Ordinance section 83 and applied it to hold that the deed operated as security rather than an outright transfer of beneficial interest.
The temple-property prescription point was decisive, but the quote only says the plea failed, the proviso is omitted, and SRC071-s34 is the wrong statute.
The court construed Notaries Ordinance section 4A and held that a notary may attest within the same judicial zone though residing in a different district.
The statement is misworded and overbroad, and the supplied quote is the District Judge's reproduced reasoning rather than the appellate court's own holding.
The court adopted the gross-ingratitude rule and applied it to the donee's assault on the donor to uphold revocation of the gift.
The quote supports the result, but the statement is too broad because the court tied ejectment to an expired notarial lease, Rent Act protection, authorized rent, and non-payment or non-deposit.

The quoted presumption was used in the Section 3 analysis, but the statement drops the companion qualification that possession begun under another title continues as such until a distinct change is proved.
The access-way rule was necessary to the partition scheme decision, but the judgment did not construe Civil Procedure Code section 754(2).
The court held that section 91A can enlarge time, but the statement omits the statutory condition of sufficient cause and the probate-objection context.
The court used this Section 431 possession-discretion principle to affirm release of the seized vehicle to the bona fide purchaser in possession.
The court adopted the encumbrance effect of the registered acquisition notice, but the provision was Finance Act section 71(2A), not SRC012-s71(1).
The quote records a fact-specific reason for quashing the quit notice, but the statement overgeneralizes it and omits the section 21A transfer, land-identity, lease-term, and ultra vires context.
The supplied proposition comes from counsel and a textbook about Fiscal's sales, while this appeal concerned a bank parate sale and intervention in a pending partition case.
The quote supports the prescriptive-title outcome, but the statement omits the co-owner context, adverse possession against other co-owners, physical demarcation, and inferred ouster.
